interactions.label: Which of the following best characterises the ebb phase of the metabolic respons

params.question: Which of the following best characterises the ebb phase of the metabolic response to injury?

answers.text: Increased metabolic rate, fever, and elevated cardiac output

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These are hallmarks of the flow phase, not the ebb phase. The flow phase is the hypermetabolic state that follows successful resuscitation.

answers.text: Lipolysis with elevated serum free fatty acids as the dominant fuel source

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fat becomes the dominant fuel during the flow phase, when the body is hypermetabolic and mobilising energy stores. The ebb phase is characterised by reduced metabolic activity.

answers.text: Decreased metabolic rate, peripheral vasoconstriction, and hypothermia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In the ebb phase, metabolic rate and oxygen consumption fall. Peripheral vessels constrict and body temperature drops as the body pulls inward to conserve resources and protect the central circulation.

answers.text: Accelerated protein synthesis and a positive nitrogen balance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Positive nitrogen balance and protein synthesis describe the anabolic sub-phase of the flow phase, when recovery is under way and muscle mass is being rebuilt.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review Cuthbertson's two-phase model. The ebb phase is the initial hypometabolic state — cold, vasoconstricted, with reduced metabolic rate and cardiac output. The flow phase follows resuscitation and is hypermetabolic.

Exactly right. The ebb phase is the initial hypometabolic, shut-down state — low metabolic rate, vasoconstriction, hypothermia, and low cardiac output. It lasts from injury until resuscitation restores blood flow.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman develops a blood glucose of 14 mmol/L twelve hours after eme

params.question: A 30-year-old woman develops a blood glucose of 14 mmol/L twelve hours after emergency splenectomy, despite no prior history of diabetes. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While dextrose infusion can contribute, the primary driver of post-injury hyperglycaemia is the hormonal stress response, not iatrogenic glucose loading.

answers.text: Insulin resistance induced by counter-regulatory hormones — cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These counter-regulatory hormones drive gluconeogenesis and induce peripheral insulin resistance, producing the 'diabetes of injury' even in previously normoglycaemic patients.

answers.text: Destruction of pancreatic beta cells by inflammatory cytokines

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Post-injury hyperglycaemia results from insulin resistance at the tissue level, not from beta-cell destruction. The pancreas still produces insulin, but peripheral tissues cannot use it effectively under the counter-regulatory hormone surge.

answers.text: Impaired hepatic glucose clearance due to hypoalbuminaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hypoalbuminaemia is part of the acute-phase response (albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant), but it does not cause hyperglycaemia. The liver actually increases gluconeogenesis during the stress response.

overallFeedback.feedback: Post-injury hyperglycaemia is driven by the counter-regulatory hormone trio — cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon — which cause gluconeogenesis and peripheral insulin resistance. This is termed the 'diabetes of injury.'

Well done. Cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon together create peripheral insulin resistance — the 'diabetes of injury.' Recognising this prevents unnecessary insulin escalation and guides nutritional support.

interactions.label: The ASA physical status classification grades which of the following?

params.question: The ASA physical status classification grades which of the following?

answers.text: The complexity and expected duration of the planned surgical procedure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ASA score grades the patient's systemic disease, not the difficulty of the planned operation. A simple procedure in a sick patient yields a high ASA grade.

answers.text: The risk of difficult airway management during intubation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Airway assessment uses the Mallampati classification, which grades the oropharyngeal view on a scale of 1 to 4. The ASA score and the Mallampati score address different questions and must never be conflated.

answers.text: The likelihood of postoperative complications specific to the procedure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While a higher ASA grade correlates with greater perioperative risk overall, the classification itself grades systemic disease severity, not procedure-specific complication rates.

answers.text: The patient's systemic disease burden, independent of the planned operation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ASA classification assesses the severity of the patient's systemic disease irrespective of the surgery planned. An E suffix is added for emergency cases.

overallFeedback.feedback: The ASA physical status classification grades the patient's systemic disease severity — from ASA I (normal healthy person) through ASA VI (brain-dead organ donor). It does not grade operative difficulty or airway anatomy.

Exactly. The ASA score classifies systemic disease from ASA I (healthy) to ASA VI (brain-dead organ donor), with an E suffix for emergencies. It is independent of surgical complexity and distinct from the Mallampati airway score.

params.question: During the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, at which point does the entire team pause to verbally confirm the patient, procedure, and surgical site?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Time-Out is performed just before the first incision. The entire team stops to verbally confirm the patient, procedure, site, anticipated critical steps, and antibiotic timing — the proven defence against wrong-site surgery.

The Sign-In confirms identity, consent, surgical site marking, allergies, and airway risk, but it occurs before anaesthesia induction. The formal team-wide pause confirming the procedure and site is the Time-Out, just before the incision.
The Sign-Out occurs after the operation is complete. It checks instrument, swab, and needle counts, confirms specimen labelling, and flags key recovery concerns — not the pre-incision confirmation.

answers.text: During the preoperative ward assessment the day before surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Preoperative ward assessment is essential for risk stratification and optimisation, but it is not one of the three formal intraoperative pauses of the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist.

overallFeedback.feedback: The WHO Checklist has three pauses: Sign-In (before anaesthesia), Time-Out (before skin incision — the team-wide confirmation of patient, procedure, and site), and Sign-Out (before the patient leaves theatre).

Well done. The Time-Out is the one-minute pause before the knife touches skin. Never let it be rushed or skipped — it is the single most effective defence against wrong-site, wrong-procedure, and wrong-patient surgery.
